text:
Chapter Twenty-Four


If Maggie were less stubborn, she would have doubled over and started complaining thoroughly about their current situation. Her calves and thighs burned with the effort of walking through the forest, and her sneakers were already soaked through with mud. But whenever Arthur would turn around to ask if she was doing okay, she would plaster a hopefully cheerful grin on her face and say something along the lines of “Of course! Why wouldn’t I be okay!” before resuming a steady stream of complaints in her head.


At least the mist had cleared, bringing with it the warm sunshine of early summer. Maggie had taken off her heavy fleece, wrapping the sleeves through her backpack straps so it hung behind her. The Wilds felt significantly less frightening when they weren’t shrouded in an impenetrable mist. Maggie even found herself admiring the forest.


Off the trail, the trees were dense, and the ground was covered in what remained of autumn’s leaves, long rotted, and pine needles. Between the pine, birch, and oak trees, scrubby bushes were filled with chittering birds. Fallen logs, covered in ivy and oyster mushrooms, crisscrossed the swampy soil. Yellow bog flowers with sharp petals and fuzzy stamens dotted the peat. Everything sprung forth with June’s impossible bright green. It was a color that Maggie forgot every year until it returned, only to be stunned by its electric hue once again.


“You know,” Maggie began, trying to disguise the labored sound of her breathing, “I was expecting to run into more ghouls out here.”


“That’s because the trail is warded.” Arthur gestured to a carving in one of the trees. Sure enough, there was a rune every ten feet or so. She remembered reading somewhere that park rangers acted as wardsmiths for the uninhabited Wilds, but she didn’t realize every trail was protected. “That’s also why we aren’t leaving the trail until we absolutely have to. I expect things will get a little bit more interesting when we cross the Dismal and have to go search for the gloaming creeper off trail.”


Arthur stopped and consulted a map he pulled from his pocket. “I think we have another forty minutes of walking before we get to the stretch of the Dismal that Dr. Silva suggested. Once we get to this warded spot here”—he pointed to a picnic area with tables and campsites—“we’ll have to leave the trail and follow the river to the east. When we’re done, we’ll come back and camp here.”


Maggie knew they would have to leave the trail eventually, but she didn’t love the idea of walking through the forest with only the rune painted over her heart for protection. They walked a little longer, both lost in thought. Maggie wasn’t sure what preoccupied Arthur, but she couldn’t stop thinking about the ghouls and wraiths and banshees that surely were lying in wait just out of sight. As she ran through the possibilities, each of them more terrifying than the last, she nearly bumped into Arthur, who had stopped in the middle of the trail.


“We’re here.” There was a slight note of what she thought might be trepidation in his voice.


Arthur slid his backpack around and reached inside, shuffling items in a way that seemed impossible for the pack’s size. Maggie watched as he pulled out an entirely too-large baseball bat and set it against a tree. “Did you install an interdimensional pocket on that thing?”


Arthur had a gleam in his eye when he looked up. “How else did you think I was packing enough supplies for our campsite tonight? You really should have let me carry your backpack.”


She tried to be annoyed at him—her back was very sweaty at this point—but she was too interested in whatever he’d done to that bag. “Can I see it?” she asked hungrily.


She’d read about the possibility of installing interdimensional storage pockets on something as small and portable as a backpack, but she’d never seen it done. A locker or closet that rarely moved, sure, but not something you could carry around. Arthur tossed the pack to her, which moved through the air as if it were empty, and she grabbed it, feeling nothing but the fabric in her hands as she swung it across her shoulders. “This is so cool!”


She brought it back around and put her arm inside up to the elbow before she felt what it contained. She stuck her head through the opening, and it was cavernous, at least the size of the large cedar chest she had at the foot of her bed.


“Why do you have wine in here, Arthur? Didn’t you call these ‘essentials’?”


“Wine is essential!” came his voice, muffled by the fabric of the pack.


She lifted her head slowly, looking up to see his satisfied grin. “Did you bring marshmallows and graham crackers, too?”


“What if I did?”


“Maybe this trek through the Wilds will be worth it if you build me a campfire and make me s’mores, then.” She stuffed her own bag into Arthur’s pack and then tossed it back to him.


He laughed as he caught it and then reached in to pull out a second bat. He threw it to her, and she was glad her reflexes were working, as she managed to catch it. “I armed the bats with repellent runes,” he explained. “Hopefully we don’t have to use them, but you won’t even have to come in contact with anything for it to work. A close swing will do the trick, so don’t worry too much about your aim.”


“Lucky for you, I played softball in high school.” Maggie swung the bat around for effect, showing off coordination she wasn’t sure she still had, since she’d last played on a team fifteen years ago. But it was just like riding a bike, apparently.


“I knew there was a reason fate put us together in that office.”


When they reached the picnic area, they stood at the edge of a small wooden bridge that crossed the Dismal. The river itself was babbling, small fish darting in the water and catching the sunlight in glimmering flashes. “The second we cross through the wards, we’re going to attract attention,” Maggie said. Arthur nodded, as if she had put to words what he was thinking in that moment, too.


Arthur pointed to a spot where the river curved to the right, about twenty feet away. “There’s a copse of trees up ahead. Let’s start there.”


Maggie took a deep breath, scanning the trees for any evidence of fantasmia that might be waiting for them. She shivered with a nervous thrill. “The faster we cross the wards, the faster we get back.”


Without another word, they both took a step off the path. They didn’t wait to see whether their crossing the wards attracted any attention, they just walked as quickly as they could through the brush toward the grove.


“Shit,” Maggie muttered when she reached the first tree. Of course it couldn’t have been so easy, but Maggie had hoped for things to go their way, for once. There wasn’t a single vine on the north side of the trees, no hint of gloaming creeper, but the soil at the tree roots was upturned. Maggie squatted and touched the damp, loamy dirt. “What did this?”


“Let’s keep going,” Arthur said, voice tight, not turning his gaze away from the trees around them. The only sound was the babbling of the Dismal and their deep breaths.


They went from tree to tree, oak after birch after pine, finding the same upturned soil. The longer they searched, the more Maggie’s hands shook. A cold wash of fear cascaded over her, like the shivering palpable fright she’d felt within the pall. An animal instinct drove her to look around the too-quiet forest, scanning the spaces between the trees. “Something isn’t right, Arthur,” she whispered, trying to keep the fear out of her voice and failing.


Arthur walked on, but Maggie couldn’t lift her foot, couldn’t bring herself to go forward. “Arthur!” She wanted to yell it, but it came out again like a whisper, and he couldn’t hear her over the sound of the Dismal’s current beside them. Ahead, he crouched down in front of a sassafras tree that was about fifteen yards away. Too far from her.


He reached down to the soil and pulled up a long vine, its leaves a dark green, nearly black. Maggie could see its stem was the earthy purple they were looking for. He looked back and began to say something, but instead his mouth contorted into a curse, and feeling came crashing into Maggie all at once.


A hissing screech echoed through the woods, a sound that seeped into Maggie like venom. Above her, a figure sped through the trees. She caught only glimpses of it through the leaves—sallow skin; deep red, animal eyes; a hand with fingernails like claws, sharpened into points, holding an already wilting bundle of gloaming creeper with dangling, exposed roots. It laid a trap for us. And the monster screeched again, revealing a mouth full of dagger teeth stained dark that made Maggie’s heart drop. Though she had heard the sound for weeks at a distance, it was nothing like the agony of hearing a banshee’s scream up close. She brought her hands up to her ears and pressed them in, trying to find some relief, but it did little to muffle the wail.


When there was finally a break in its cry, Maggie looked around and saw Arthur on the ground, holding his hands against the sides of his head. He grimaced in pain and Maggie didn’t think, she just ran toward him, tripping over roots and underbrush. She urged herself forward, trying to get to Arthur before the banshee, and lifting her bat in a fluid motion. It was the only graceful thing she managed, though, as low branches scraped across her skin, and she nearly skidded on a bank of mud.


The creature dropped its gloaming creeper trap and hovered above Arthur, a beast over its prey. It reached down slowly, whatever covering it wore over its skin hanging in filthy tatters. Long nails scraped against the bark above Arthur’s head, just barely brushing his hair in a sinister taunt. He cringed and scooted away from the tree trunk, clambering for his bat. He didn’t tear his eyes away from the banshee, which was slowly making its way toward him with hands outstretched as he hissed, “Get back to the path!”


Despite her fear, Maggie managed to scoff. As if she would leave him here, abandon him when he hadn’t abandoned her. He was ridiculous.


With a final lurch forward, the banshee reached a hand out toward Arthur, ready to drag its claws down his cheek, but then there was the undeniable snap of magic, and the banshee was retreating, hissing and cradling its hand as if it had been burned. Her rune had worked.


Arthur kicked a leg up and managed to snag the banshee’s leg, enraging the beast even more until it was screeching again. “Get back, Maggie!” Arthur yelled once more, getting up on his knees with enough purchase to swing his bat. With another one of those horrendous hisses through its fangs that Maggie swore she could feel in her chest, the banshee grabbed the bat and tugged it out of Arthur’s hands, tossing it into the Dismal. “Fuck,” he cursed. “Throw me your bat!” he gasped, trying to catch his breath.


“Absolutely not!” Maggie shouted, half hoping the banshee would turn its attention toward her. She was upright and uninjured. She’d been farther away from the banshee as it had screeched, and it seemed to have made a difference in how affected they both were. “Only one of us has played in an all-star softball game, and obviously it wasn’t you.” Maggie stepped back on her heel, cocking her elbow, and allowed muscle memory from years of practice to completely take over. “If you think I’m going to let you take credit for fighting off a banshee like you did the day the pall fell out of some sort of misguided, self-righteous belief that I’m a damsel…”


“This is not the time!” Arthur yelled, his eyes wide as the banshee came careening back. When it was close enough, Maggie swung the bat as hard as she could, missing the beast by a hair’s breadth, but it was enough. It shrieked, the force of the magic contained in the rune on the bat pinning the banshee against a tree trunk.


Maggie reached a hand down to Arthur and yanked him to standing. Ridiculously, he had a huge grin on his face. “Come on,” she said, already beginning to jog back to the warded pathway.


“I got the gloaming creeper!” He grinned even wider, holding it up to show her.


“And almost got killed in the process,” she muttered, turning to see if the banshee had been released from its invisible shackles. It was still pinned by the magic, frothing and writhing against the force that kept it down. “How long will that magic hold?”


“Not long.” They were nearly there, the wards shimmering in the late-afternoon sun. Arthur reached for Maggie as they ran, tugging her through the wards, before they collapsed over the line that marked the path. He caught her in his arms, and they tumbled together to the ground with an oof and a sharp pain in Maggie’s hip. She had landed halfway onto Arthur’s chest, his hard body, all lean and muscle, beneath her. Incomprehensibly, he was laughing. Giggling.


She leaned up on her elbow and furrowed her brow, which seemed to make him laugh harder. “Nothing about that was funny.”


“You’re very right about that,” he said, nearly out of breath from the running and the bubbling laughter. “You were spectacular. I don’t know why you were ever frightened.” After a moment, he added, “Thank you. I would have been a banshee’s dinner if it weren’t for you.”


Abruptly, Arthur’s eyes widened, and Maggie turned to see the banshee had pulled free of its invisible shackles to follow their scent. Banshees couldn’t see well in daylight, and their presence was masked by the runes on the path, but they both held their breath. With a huff that felt too human for Maggie’s comfort, the banshee vanished into the trees. After a moment, Maggie realized she was still half on top of Arthur and his fingers were tight around her arm, sure and safe.


She cleared her throat, and he let her go so she could stand and brush off her leggings, looking warily toward the sun that was close to setting. “What happens at night?” she asked.


Arthur came up beside her and took the bat she still gripped in her hands, his touch gentle. “Nothing,” he said calmly. “We camp. We eat and have a drink and tell ghost stories around the fire.”


“Please, no more ghosts.”


“Fine. Tell me stories about Branagh.” He paused. “About enemies who become lovers.”


She swallowed. She wanted to give in to what was clearly flirting, but she bit her lip. “Won’t the banshees be able to see us at night?”


“The wards will keep them away. We’re safe now,” he said. “I promise.”



—


Maggie sat on an old picnic table covered in engravings left by previous campers while Arthur unpacked his supplies. He set a rune afire in the middle of the small, warded circle until it burned with a pleasant heat, and then set up faefire torches that burned heatless flame. They doubled as protection and cast the clearing in a charming, flickering light that did as much to settle Maggie’s nerves as the wards themselves. Maggie had finally caught her breath, but she couldn’t stop looking for the banshee in the darkening forest that surrounded their small, illuminated campsite.


She traced the engravings on the picnic table and watched Arthur. He had removed his fleece long ago, and she was trying to pretend she wasn’t watching the muscles in his arms flex as he lifted supplies out of his pack. There were now two large nylon bags sitting on the packed dirt, along with a clear box she could see contained food, but he was still digging around in the interdimensional pocket. He swore and then looked through the supplies again.


“What is it?” Maggie asked, standing to come and help.


He looked through the pack one more time and shook his head. “It’s nothing. I just forgot something, but it’s not important.”


“What can I do?” she asked.


He pointed to the box of food. “Want to unpack that on the picnic table while I organize our tents?”


“I brought some food, too,” she said as she set the box on the table, thinking of the now-squished peanut butter and jelly sandwiches in her small bag. Inside the box were supplies to make a charcuterie spread, with several different kinds of cheese, grapes, and salami, and the bottle of red wine. He’d even remembered a corkscrew. “Um, never mind,” she said, realizing quickly how much effort he’d put into packing their dinner.


“I’m thirty-five years old. I may like to camp, but I do not need to rough it.” He clicked the tent poles together expertly and threaded them through the nylon until it resembled something tent shaped.


“This is more my speed,” Maggie admitted, setting out the cheese and fruit on a wooden board that was also conveniently packed in the box.


Soon, two tents were set up, side by side. Maggie had been preparing herself all day to sleep in the same tent as Arthur. And all of the previous night. Now that she saw she wouldn’t have to share, she couldn’t deny the tinge of disappointment she felt. “This one is yours,” Arthur said as he opened the zipper and pinned back the door. A small lantern hung from the top of the tent, and there was a sleeping bag and pillow inside. “Now, can we please eat? Something about being almost maimed by a banshee has made me famished.”

facts.fact: 徒步逞强：嘴上 Of course 脑内抱怨不断；雾散后初夏阳光照进 Wilds——六月的绿年年电到她。
facts.anchor: stunned by its electric hue once again

facts.fact: 步道结界：每十英尺树刻符文（rangers 兼职无人区 wardsmith）；计划到 warded 点再离道沿河。
异次元背包：轻若无物、内藏洞天；酒 essential；还有 marshmallows 与 graham crackers。
双球棒防身符文：挥近即生效不用瞄准；她 15 年前全明星垒球——命运梗自爆。
facts.anchor: I armed the bats with repellent runes

facts.fact: banshee 伏击：离道第一片林全是翻起的土（藤被挖走）——它布了 trap；嘶鸣如毒液渗入。
facts.anchor: It laid a trap for us

facts.fact: 危局：他捂头跪地、banshee 悬于其上如兽俯猎物；他喊 Get back to the path——她 scoff 不丢下他。
她拒交球棒：全明星垒球是我打的；别想像 pall 那天抢功把我当 damsel。
facts.anchor: Only one of us has played in an all-star softball game

facts.fact: 反杀：脚跟后撤屈肘抬臂肌肉记忆接管——挥棒差之毫厘正中，符文之力钉敌上树。
facts.anchor: muscle memory from years of practice

facts.fact: 他拿回 gloaming creeper咧嘴傻笑；扑过结界摔作一团他咯咯笑：You were spectacular。
营地：charcuterie 套装（35 岁不爱吃苦）；两顶帐篷并排——她藏住一丝失望。
facts.anchor: I do not need to rough it

facts.fact: 火边调情：讲 Branagh 的故事吧——冤家变恋人那种；她咬唇岔开问夜间安全。
